cells.tense: Here, the clearing is already under way, and you have a hand on the knife and a hand on the pen.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: Before you plan what to refine, do the plainest version of the work — the way you first learned it — and see where it's already sharper than you remembered.
cells.core:
You know a thing by the pull toward it, not by a plan, and you can tell the difference between wanting the light and wanting to have arrived. When something you built on a guess shows you it was a guess, you drop it — you don't argue with it for a year first. That is rarer than it sounds. The clearing comes from something you actually saw, and the space it leaves gets used.

The risk is that you admire the clearing and call that the work. What keeps it honest is small and repetitive — the same piece, done again, made a little truer. Not a new direction. The plain version comes first, before the plans get to rearrange it, and doing it that way shows you what the work actually is. Come back on the days it looks ordinary. The pull stays lit by attention, not by flash.
cells.sheetLine: The clearing served you. Do the plain version first today.
cells.verb: cutting away what stopped being true, all at once
cells.place: in the pull toward the light you're steering by

cells.tense: What has not happened yet is being torn down in advance, and you are bracing for the door before anyone has knocked.
cells.act: join the practice the others keep
cells.ask: Go sit in one practice the others have kept longer than you've been watching — a class, a meeting, a service — and don't take it apart in your head while you're there.
cells.core:
Where you steer by the light you want, the tearing down starts outrunning the truth that would justify it. You can see what's hollow in a thing before it has had a chance to hold — and right now you see it everywhere, in arrangements that were still carrying weight. Old rules, old routines, the way a week is built. Some of what falls is real. Some of it is the room losing its walls before you know where you're standing.

You don't need less vision. You need one thing that isn't yours to take apart. Go where the practice already exists and the others have held it steady without you — a class, a meeting, a service, something that runs whether or not you show up. Sit in it this week and let it be what it is. What you want to clear will still be there when you come back. You'll just be standing on something.

cells.tense: You were at that door a long time ago, and some part of you is still standing in front of it.
cells.act: put a date, a place, a container on it
cells.ask: Give something you keep holding up a when and a where and a line where it stops, so you can tell whether anything living is still inside.
cells.core:
Things you once decided still have your weight on them. A rule, a role, an arrangement, the way a week is supposed to run — some of them stopped being true a while back, and you haven't noticed, because noticing would mean letting them go, and the light you steer by is somewhere past what you've already built. So the hands don't leave the old thing. That isn't a failure of strength. The knack for cutting clean is in you; where you're standing now, it is standing down.

Don't try to fell anything today. Give one of them a when and a where and a line where it stops. That's not a verdict, just a shape. Once it has boundaries you can tell whether anything living is still inside, or only your grip on the outside. Nothing has to happen yet. The shape holds long enough for you to look, and the next clear morning it will still be there.

cells.tense: Something is already giving way, and you are writing it down as nothing in particular.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Follow the pull you already feel toward one thing — a call, a message, an hour kept — and afterward keep a note, in your own hand, that you went.
cells.core:
You've been making openings and filing them under circumstances. A conversation where something loosened, a decision that changed the shape of a week, a thing let go of because it simply didn't come up again — from the outside it looks like the wind did it. You did it. The pull toward what you want is steering you; it has been for a while. What's missing is that you don't know your own hand is on the wheel, so the clearing still reads as something that happened to you.

Start where the pull is already loud. Not the plan — the step itself, today, toward the thing. A call, a message, an hour kept. Then don't put it down to timing. Keep the note the other way, in your own hand: went there. The rest of the clearing can wait. What's owed first is the record of your own moving.
